title: Wittgenstein's Tractarian Ontology
description: A Lean 4 formalization of the structural core of Wittgenstein's Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus: objects, states of affairs, worlds, propositions, and truth-functionality. Proves compositionality, independence, and the saying/showing distinction — that any proposition expressing a world-independent property must be trivially a tautology or contradiction.

mathlibDependencies.description: Law of excluded middle (classical logic axiom)
De Morgan: not(P and Q) iff notP or notQ

originalContributions: Formal ontology mapping Tractatus propositions to Lean types
Truth-functional compositionality theorem via structural induction
Elementary independence theorem witnessing the Sachverhalt/world correspondence
Saying/showing distinction: world-independent properties collapse to tautology or contradiction
Corrected Proposition 7: replaces false existential with the correct triviality theorem
Philosophical annotations bridging formal verification and Wittgensteinian philosophy
meta.assumptions: No axiom declarations and no structure-encoded assumptions. All theorems fully verified. Uses classical logic (Classical.em) throughout, matching Wittgenstein's bivalent semantics.

overview.historicalContext: The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) is Wittgenstein's only book-length philosophical work published in his lifetime. It presents a logical atomist ontology: the world consists of facts (obtaining states of affairs), propositions picture possible states of affairs, and all meaningful propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions. The work culminates in proposition 6.54 — the famous ladder that must be thrown away — and the closing injunction: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'
overview.problemStatement: Can the structural core of the Tractatus — its ontology of objects, states of affairs, worlds, and truth-functional propositions — be faithfully formalized in a modern proof assistant? Can the saying/showing distinction (TLP 4.12-4.1212) be given precise mathematical content? What is captured by formalization, and what necessarily escapes?
overview.proofStrategy: We define types for objects (opaque), states of affairs (abstract), and worlds (predicates on states of affairs). Propositions form an inductive type with elementary, negation, and conjunction constructors. All other connectives are derived. A recursive evaluation function maps propositions to truth values relative to worlds. We prove compositionality, independence, connective semantics, and the saying/showing distinction: any proposition whose truth value is world-independent must be a tautology or contradiction.
keyInsights: The world-as-predicate encoding makes elementary independence trivially true — the assignment IS the world
Truth-functional compositionality follows by structural induction on the proposition type
The formalization necessarily works at the metalevel — we prove theorems ABOUT propositions in Lean, which is precisely the kind of thing Wittgenstein says can only be shown, not said
Classical logic (excluded middle) is used throughout, matching Wittgenstein's bivalent semantics
The saying/showing distinction is formalized as a triviality theorem: world-independent content can only be 'said' by tautologies or contradictions, which say nothing specific
prerequisites: Familiarity with Lean 4 syntax (inductive types, pattern matching)
Some acquaintance with the Tractatus is helpful but not required

sections.title: Preamble
sections.summary: Module imports and documentation header introducing the formalization scope.

sections.title: Objects (TLP 2.02)
sections.summary: Objects as an abstract variable type — simple, structureless entities.

sections.title: States of Affairs (TLP 2.01)
sections.summary: States of affairs (Sachverhalte) as an abstract type of possible combinations.

sections.title: Worlds (TLP 1, 1.1, 2.04)
sections.summary: Worlds as predicates determining which states of affairs obtain.

sections.title: Propositions (TLP 4.21, 5)
sections.summary: Inductive type for propositions: elementary, negation, conjunction.

sections.title: Derived Connectives (TLP 5.101)
sections.summary: Disjunction, implication, biconditional, and NAND defined from negation and conjunction.

sections.title: Semantic Evaluation (TLP 2.21, 4.06)
sections.summary: Recursive truth-value evaluation of propositions relative to worlds.

sections.title: Tautology and Contradiction (TLP 4.46, 6.1)
sections.summary: Definitions of tautology (true in all worlds) and contradiction (false in all worlds).

sections.title: Theorems
sections.summary: Thirteen theorems establishing compositionality, independence, bivalence, connective semantics, and functional completeness.

sections.title: The Saying/Showing Distinction (TLP 4.12-4.1212)
sections.summary: Formalizes the structural shadow of Wittgenstein's saying/showing distinction. Proves that world-constant propositions are trivial (tautology or contradiction), that expressing a world-independent property forces triviality, and that non-trivial propositions must vary across worlds.

sections.title: The Limits of Formalization (TLP 6.54, 7)
sections.summary: Proposition 7 formalized as the triviality theorem: any attempt to express a world-independent truth in the object language produces a trivial proposition. Philosophical commentary on the gap between formal matching and meaningful expression.

conclusion.summary: We have formalized the ontological skeleton of the Tractatus and a structural analogue of its most philosophically distinctive claim: the saying/showing distinction. All nineteen theorems are fully proved with no sorries. The culminating result — that any proposition expressing a world-independent property must be trivially a tautology or contradiction — gives precise mathematical content to TLP 4.1212: 'What can be shown cannot be said.'
conclusion.implications: This demonstrates that the formal core of the Tractatus — often dismissed as merely philosophical rather than mathematical — admits precise statement and machine-verified proof. The saying/showing formalization reveals that the original Proposition 7 statement (existence of inexpressible Props) was mathematically incorrect: in classical logic every Prop is expressible by a tautology or contradiction. The correct insight is that such expression is trivial — the same tautology expresses every truth. This triviality, not inexpressibility, is the formal content of Wittgenstein's silence.
openQuestions: Could dependent types better capture TLP 2.0141 — that an object's form IS its combinatorial possibility?
Can the triviality result be strengthened to capture information-theoretic content — that tautologies carry zero information about which specific metalinguistic fact holds?
How does this propositional framework relate to Wittgenstein's later rejection of logical atomism?

references.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Translated by C.K. Ogden and F.P. Ramsey. The numbering system (1, 1.1, 2.01, etc.) indicates logical dependencies between propositions.

references.title: Introduction to the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Russell's introduction — which Wittgenstein reportedly disliked — interprets the Tractatus within the framework of Principia Mathematica.

references.title: A set of five independent postulates for Boolean algebras
references.venue: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 14
references.note: Introduces the Sheffer stroke (NAND), which Wittgenstein references in TLP 5.5 as showing all truth-functions reduce to a single operation.

references.title: The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages
references.note: Tarski's undefinability theorem (1936) is the semantic descendant of what Wittgenstein gestures at in TLP 4.12-4.1212 (1921). Our triviality result is a baby version of Tarski's result for a propositional object language.

mainTheorems.name: tautology_is_world_invariant
mainTheorems.description: A proposition is a tautology iff it holds in every world (TLP 6.1)
mainTheorems.leanType: (forall w : World S, p.eval w) <-> IsTautology p

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality
mainTheorems.description: Worlds agreeing on elementaries agree on all compounds (TLP 5)
mainTheorems.leanType: forall (p : Proposition S) (w1 w2 : World S), (forall s, w1 s <-> w2 s) -> (p.eval w1 <-> p.eval w2)

mainTheorems.name: elementary_independence
mainTheorems.description: Any truth-value assignment to states of affairs is realizable (TLP 2.061)
mainTheorems.leanType: exists w : World S, forall s : S, w s <-> assignment s

mainTheorems.name: excluded_middle_tautology
mainTheorems.description: p or not p is a tautology (TLP 4.46)

mainTheorems.name: world_constant_taut_or_contra
mainTheorems.description: A world-constant proposition must be a tautology or contradiction (TLP 4.46)
mainTheorems.leanType: forall (q : Proposition S) [Nonempty S], (forall w1 w2, q.eval w1 <-> q.eval w2) -> IsTautology q or IsContradiction q

mainTheorems.name: saying_showing_triviality
mainTheorems.description: Any proposition expressing a world-independent property is trivial (TLP 4.1212)
mainTheorems.leanType: forall (q : Proposition S) (P : Prop) [Nonempty S], (forall w, q.eval w <-> P) -> IsTautology q or IsContradiction q

mainTheorems.name: proposition_seven
mainTheorems.description: Expressing a world-independent truth forces triviality (TLP 7)
mainTheorems.leanType: forall (q : Proposition S) (P : Prop) [Nonempty S], (forall w, q.eval w <-> P) -> IsTautology q or IsContradiction q
